There are three types of satellite used by GPS, Low Earth Orbit (LEO), Medium Earth Orbit (MEO) and Geostationary Orbit (GEO). 

Leos are about 20-25 miles above the Earth and go around the Earth once each day as the Earth rotates. You will notice that once in a while your phone or your phone’s GPS will give you an error that doesn’t involve a circle that the GPS uses to calculate your location. MEOs are in the middle of the orbit of the Earth and go around about every hour. They don’t have a high frequency so your GPS won’t always report the location accurately. 

GEOs are in the highest orbit, which means they don’t move from side to side, but instead they are stationary. So usually your phone will always report the correct location for you, even when you move from one part of the world to another. 

Your phone also uses the Global Positioning Service (GPS) to find nearby Wi-Fi hotspots and Wi-Fi networks, or use your phone’s location to determine if your phone is in proximity to a Wi-Fi network. If you’re in a place where there are no WI-FI hotspots available, your phone gets your location from the GPS, but as explained above, sometimes the GPS receiver may not get all the required and accurate data.
